newsitem.title: MALDIVES: Pakistan, India agree concrete steps at talks.
newsitem.headline: Pakistan, India agree concrete steps at talks.

text.p: The prime ministers of India and Pakistan on Monday took the most far-reaching steps towards normalising relations since the two regional foes launched fresh peace talks earlier this year.

Following are the measures which Pakistani Prime Minister Nawaz Sharif and his Indian counterpart, Inder Kumar Gujral, agreed at a scenic Kurumba beach hotel in the Indian Ocean archipelago of the Maldives during 90 minutes of talks:
- Pakistan and India will set up a telephone hotline between the two prime ministers. It would be in addition to a hot line between the two nations' military directors-general.
- The two leaders instructed their foreign secretaries -- the highest ranking civil servants in the foreign ministries -- to set up working groups to discuss outstanding issues.
Indian Foreign Secretary Salman Haider said he and his Pakistani counterpart, Shamshad Ahmed, would begin the task of identifying the subjects for discussion at talks set for the latter half of June.
Ahmed said the working groups would address all outstanding issues between the two countries, including the "core issue" of divided Kashmir.
- The leaders decided that all civilian nationals held prisoner on either sides would be freed.
Haider said they included some 190 Indian fisherman held in Pakistan and 210 to 220 Pakistani fishermen in Indian jails. Some civilian prisoners were jailed after overstaying their visas.
The decision to release the civilian prisoners will be implemented immediately.
- The two sides discussed the possible sale of surplus electrical power from Pakistan to energy-starved northern India, Haider said.
- The two leaders will take steps to encourage greater people-to-people contact through the easing of visa restrictions and a requirement to report to police.
- The two said diplomats should be treated "in a civilised manner", Haider said. In the past, some diplomats and diplomatic staff have said they were physically beaten.
- The foreign ministries of the two countries should not make provocative statements against each other, Haider said.
